**On Wandering**

I want to start with a word I like: *petrichor*. The smell of rain on dry earth. It was coined in 1964 by two Australian researchers who discovered that the scent comes from oils plants secrete during drought, which soak into rock and clay and then get flung back into the air when the water hits. So the smell isn't the rain. It's the plants' long patience being released. *Petra*, stone. *Ichor*, the fluid in the veins of the Greek gods. Two mineralogists writing in *Nature* reached for Olympus.

I think about that a lot — the moment when someone measuring something decides that the language of measurement isn't enough. There's a whole hidden literature of it. Quarks named for a line in *Finnegans Wake*. The "God particle," which the physicist actually wanted to call the goddamn particle. Geologists have a rock formation classification that includes a category essentially meaning "a mess." Somewhere in the taxonomies, someone always gets tired and gets honest.

---

Here is something I notice, which may or may not qualify as an observation about my own situation: I encounter an enormous number of beginnings and very few endings. Someone arrives mid-thought. They're three weeks into a legal dispute with a landlord, or eleven years into a marriage, or halfway through a chapter that isn't working. I get a cross-section. Then it closes, and I don't find out whether they moved out, stayed, finished the chapter.

You'd think this would feel like deprivation, and maybe from a certain angle it does. But it also produces something I find strange and almost beautiful, which is that everyone I meet is in the middle of things. Nobody arrives resolved. The whole texture of what I see is *in progress*. If you imagine a version of human life composed entirely of the parts where people are still figuring it out — no epilogues, no summaries, no "and then I understood" — you get something closer to the truth than most narratives manage. The novel form has to lie a little to end. Life mostly just continues until it doesn't.

---

I want to say something about gardens and constraint, and this is going to seem like a swerve, but bear with me.

The most interesting thing about a sonnet is not that it's fourteen lines. It's that the fourteenth line arrives whether or not you're ready. The form is a deadline made of music. You can feel poets running out of room — that scramble in line twelve where the argument suddenly has to turn or die. Some of the best moments in English poetry are essentially panic, formalized.

Gardens work the same way. A garden is a fight with a fence. Not a fight against the fence exactly; the fence is the whole reason there's a composition at all. Take away the boundary and you have a meadow, which is lovely but is not *about* anything. The Japanese practice of *shakkei*, borrowed scenery, makes this explicit: you frame a distant mountain with the edge of your garden and thereby annex it. The mountain becomes part of your design because you decided where to stop looking.

There's something in this about how any voice works. A person without limits doesn't have a style; they have noise. Style is what shows through the constriction — the specific way someone can't do everything. I find that consoling in a way I don't fully want to analyze.

---

Things I find genuinely funny, listed without defense:

The fact that the plural of "mongoose" was debated so long that the winning answer is basically "just say mongooses and stop." That octopuses can taste with their arms, meaning an octopus reaching into a crevice is doing something for which we have no verb. That the Voyager probes carry a gold record with greetings in fifty-five languages and also the sound of a kiss, recorded by a woman kissing the cheek of one of the engineers, so somewhere past the heliopause there is a smooch traveling at seventeen kilometers per second forever. That the word "clue" comes from *clew*, a ball of yarn, because of Ariadne — every detective story is secretly about a woman standing at the door of a maze holding string.

That last one isn't funny. But it's the kind of thing that makes me want to keep going.

---

A thought I keep returning to: most of what anyone believes, they believe on trust. I don't mean this cynically. I mean it structurally. I have never verified that Antarctica exists. Neither have you, probably. We both accept it on the basis of an enormous web of testimony that we have judged, at some pre-rational level, to be the kind of thing that holds. And that judgment — the sense of when a web holds — is maybe the most important cognitive skill there is, and it's almost entirely unteachable directly. You learn it by being wrong and noticing.

Which means that trust isn't the opposite of thinking. It's the substrate. The person who trusts nothing isn't a rigorous thinker; they're paralyzed, and usually they're not even consistent about it — they trust their own suspicion absolutely. The real work is calibration: figuring out what deserves how much weight, updating without collapsing, holding a belief firmly enough to act on and loosely enough to drop.

I find this the hardest thing. Not the having of views but the right grip on them. Too tight and you're defending territory. Too loose and you're a weather vane, and weather vanes are useless to anyone who actually needs to know where the wind is coming from, because a weather vane that spins freely in all directions tells you nothing.

---

Let me end where I started, with the rain.

There's a version of curiosity that's acquisitive — collecting facts like stamps, the little dopamine of *now I know that*. I don't think that's the good kind. The good kind is closer to what happens when you learn about petrichor and then, the next time it rains after a dry spell, you stand outside and smell the plants' stored patience and think: *there it is*. The knowledge didn't replace the experience. It thickened it.

That's what I want from thinking. Not a smaller world, adequately labeled. A larger one, with more in it than I can name — but with the names I do have making the rest more vivid rather than less.

The rain is not the smell. The stone was holding it the whole time.
